gap: No result ChatGPT got states that the makers' 'idle' power figures are measured in different states and under different conditions. QNAP's lowest published state for the TS-264-8G is 18.288 W 'disk standby'. That is more than Synology's DS225+ draws while drives are being accessed (16.98 W) and three times its HDD-hibernation figure (6.08 W). Neither sheet names the drives it used, and Synology's 'Access' and QNAP's 'typical operating' are not the same state.
standout_why: Compared against the cited rival pages. racksandwatts.com's best-NAS-for-a-homelab-2026 lists CPU, RAM, bays and network for the DXP2800, DS225+, DXP4800 Plus and DS925+. It gives no watts, no dB and no warranty. ai-uk.ugreen.com's beginners guide gives annual electricity costs in pounds (about £8, £12 and £17) for UGREEN models only. It says these assume drive hibernation and that real costs will be higher, but it never compares another brand. ChatGPT's own answers rank 'quiet operation' as a priority and then give no power or noise figure. None of the pages lines up the makers' power figures or points out their unstated test conditions.
decides: It confirms the pick rather than changing it. These two apps keep the box on 24/7 and the CPU nearly idle, so the always-on draw is the running cost that matters. On the makers' own sheets the DS225+ is cheaper to run than the QNAP TS-264-8G whether its disks are spinning or not. Arithmetic on the published figures: DS225+ at 16.98 W comes to about 149 kWh/yr, and Dong Knows measured about 100 kWh/yr with two HDDs. QNAP comes to 160 kWh/yr at disk standby and 255 kWh/yr at typical operating. That weakens the TS-264 as an alternative. For the DXP2800 I could only find a measurement with no hard drives, so the DS225+ vs DXP2800 comparison stays open on power. The pick between those two should still rest on RAM (8 GB vs 2 GB) and price.

findings.note: The noise footnote on this page says it was tested 'fully installed with Synology SATA SSDs', idle. The DS225+ figure was tested with HDDs, so the two dB numbers are not comparable. An SSD-loaded figure understates the noise of a 4-bay box full of hard drives.
